newsitem.title: NORWAY: Nobel Peace Prize winner sees thaw with Jakarta.
newsitem.headline: Nobel Peace Prize winner sees thaw with Jakarta.

text.p: Nobel Peace Prize laureate Jose Ramos Horta, a self-exiled East Timor independence campaigner, said on Wednesday he believed Jakarta would one day listen to his proposals for peace in the Indonesia-ruled territory.
Ramos Horta shared the 1996 peace prize with Roman Catholic Bishop Carlos Belo of East Timor on Tuesday to the dismay of Indonesia, which boycotted the award ceremony in Oslo.
The Jakarta government has condemned the Norwegian Nobel Committee's decision to include the veteran resistance leader in the prestigious prize.
But Ramos Horta, 48, speaking with reporters after seeing Norwegian Foreign Minister Bjoern Tore Godal, was not discouraged by the Indonesian snub.

"In the long run they will come around and talk with us, like South Africa in the end had to talk with Mandela," he said in a reference to South African President Nelson Mandela, a 1993 Nobel Peace Prize co-winner.
"Everywhere, regimes first don't want to talk with opposition leaders. I am ready to go to Jakarta tomorrow if they want."

Nobel Committee chairman Francis Sejersted, who presented the laureates with the $1.12 million prize, said they were awarded "for their long-lasting efforts to achieve a just and peaceful solution to the 20-year-old conflict in East Timor".

Indonesia invaded East Timor in December 1975 and declared the territory its 27th province seven months later in a move still not recognised by the United Nations which regards old colonial master Portugal as the administering power.

In his Nobel speech, Ramos Horta presented proposals for gradual East Timor self-determination, sharply criticised the Indonesian stance but called on Jakarta to enter a dialogue on a peace settlement.

"As much as I wanted to be non-confrontational I had to say certain things because otherwise I would be betraying the people in East Timor," said Ramos Horta, who lost three of his brothers and a sister after the invasion.
Indonesian Foreign Minister Ali Alatas, speaking in Jakarta on Tuesday, distanced himself from Ramos Horta.
"Dialogue with whom and between whom?" Alatas asked reporters. "If it is with Ramos Horta, there is the AETD (the U.N.-sponsored All-inclusive East Timorese Dialogue)," he said.
"The problem (of East Timor) must be solved by Indonesia and Portugal and it cannot be solved by other groups," he said.

Lisbon and Jakarta have held periodic but largely unproductive meetings under the auspices of the U.N. in an attempt to resolve differences over East Timor, where clashes between government and guerrilla soldiers still occur.
Godal said Norway, which helped broker the 1993 Israel-PLO peace pact, was not thinking of assuming a mediating role on East Timor but would host peace talks if need be.
"I have offered to Alatas that Norway could host meetings in order for a Timorese dialogue to take place," he said. "The answer was reasonably positive but non-committal."
"If the parties want to bring Norway into this work we would do it. But you need two parties to wish this for it to happen."
